title: "Get started with jlbind"

---

jlbind lets an R package call Julia code without starting a separate Julia
session. It compiles Julia code into a shared library using
[JuliaC.jl](https://github.com/JuliaLang/JuliaC.jl), then exposes Julia
functions to R through native `.Call()` routines.

This vignette explains how to add Julia functions to your own R package with
jlbind. An R package that uses jlbind is called a *client*. For how jlbind
compares with other ways of calling Julia from R, see
[Performance](https://bjarkehautop.github.io/jlbind/vignettes/articles/performance.html).

An R process can load only one compiled Julia library[^privatize], so jlbind
compiles the Julia code of *all* installed clients into one shared library,
which each user builds with `jlbind::install_library()`. Your client therefore
shares Julia dependency versions with every other client the user has installed.
[Using packages built on jlbind](using-clients.html) describes how this works
and what your users need to do; your README should tell them to run
`jlbind::install_library()` after installing your package.

For complete, working examples, see the two small clients that jlbind's tests
build:
[`hellojl`](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/jlbind/tree/main/tests/clients/hellojl),
which passes plain values, and
[`counterjl`](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/jlbind/tree/main/tests/clients/counterjl),
which keeps Julia objects in R (see [Julia objects in R](#julia-objects-in-r)).

[^privatize]: JuliaC can *privatize* a library, giving it its own copy of the
    Julia runtime, but jlbind doesn't use this. Each client would then load its
    own runtime, adding tens of MB per client on disk, its own garbage-collected
    heap and threads in memory, and Julia objects couldn't be passed between
    clients. Privatization also doesn't work on Windows yet
    ([JuliaC.jl#151](https://github.com/JuliaLang/JuliaC.jl/pull/151)).

## Set up

You need [Julia](https://julialang.org/install/) 1.13 or later. From your R
package's directory, run:

```r
jlbind::use_jlbind()
```

This creates the files and configuration needed to connect the package to
jlbind:

- `inst/julia/`, containing a Julia binding package named after the R package
  with a `Bindings` suffix (for example, `MyPkgBindings`), including an example
  function.
- `src/jlbind.c` and `src/entrypoints.h`, which register the native routines,
  and a rule in `src/Makevars` that recompiles `jlbind.c` whenever
  `entrypoints.h` changes.
- `R/jlbind-wrappers.R`, with an R function for each Julia function the binding
  package declares.
- `R/jlbind.R`, which calls `jlbind::bind_client()` from `.onLoad()` and
  includes the roxygen tag for `useDynLib()`.
- The `Config/jlbind`, `Imports: jlbind` and
  `SystemRequirements: Julia (>= 1.13)` fields in `DESCRIPTION`.
- A `.jlbind/` directory for development builds, added to `.Rbuildignore` and
  `.gitignore`.

If your package already defines `.onLoad()`, add `jlbind::bind_client(pkgname)`
to the existing function yourself. Then run `devtools::document()` to update
`NAMESPACE`.

::: {.callout-important title="Give the Julia binding package a unique name"}
All clients are compiled into one library, so binding package names must be
unique across all jlbind clients. The default, the R package name with a
`Bindings` suffix, ensures this.
:::

## Declare Julia functions

Inside the binding package, declare each function that R should be able to call
using `@rcall`. Each declaration specifies the argument types and return type
expected by the binding.

For example:

```julia
module MyPkgBindings

using JLBind

greet(name::String) = "Hello, " * name * "!"
shift(x::Vector{Float64}, by::Union{Nothing,Float64}) =
    by === nothing ? x : x .+ by

@rcall greet(name::String)::String
@rcall shift(x::Vector{Float64}, by::Union{Nothing,Float64} = nothing)::Vector{Float64}

end
```

The binding package is an ordinary Julia package. Declare its dependencies in
`Project.toml` and import them as usual.

::: {.callout-important title="Write `@rcall` declarations literally at the top level"}
jlbind finds `@rcall` declarations by scanning the source files, not by running
them, so write them literally at the top level of the module.
:::

## Call them from R

Whenever you add or change `@rcall` declarations, regenerate the native routine
list:

```r
jlbind::update_entrypoints()
```

This generates an R function for each declaration, in `R/jlbind-wrappers.R`:

```r
greet <- function(name) .Call(C_greet, name)
shift <- function(x, by = NULL) .Call(C_shift, x, by)
```

Defaults in the declaration (literal numbers, strings, `true`, `false` or
`nothing`) become R defaults.

To export or document a generated function, use a roxygen block on `NULL` with
`@name greet` in another file. To add R code around a call, declare the Julia
function with a `jl_` prefix, e.g. `@rcall jl_shift(...)`, and write `shift()`
yourself.

## Build and test locally

During development, you usually want to build the library from your package's
source rather than from the installed clients. Run:

```r
jlbind::build_library()
devtools::load_all()
```

By default, `build_library()` writes the library to `.jlbind/` in your package's
source directory. When you load the package with `devtools::load_all()`, jlbind
uses this development library instead of the one created by `install_library()`.

Once `.jlbind/` exists, `devtools::load_all()` rebuilds it when your binding
package's files or your package's version have changed since it was built.

::: {.callout-note title="The development library is only used when your package loads first"}
The `.jlbind/` library is used only if your package is the first jlbind client
loaded in the R session. A library that has loaded cannot be replaced, so after
changing your Julia code, restart R; the next `load_all()` rebuilds it.
:::

If you need to use a library stored elsewhere, set the `JLBIND_LIBRARY`
environment variable to its path before loading the package.

You can also test against an unreleased version of a Julia dependency by
providing a local checkout through `develop`:

```r
jlbind::build_library(develop = "~/dev/SomePackage.jl")
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Pin the dependency versions"}
Include a `Manifest.toml` next to the binding package's `Project.toml` with the
Julia dependency versions known to compile with your package. [CRAN's
policy](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/policies.html) asks that
downloaded libraries be a fixed version rather than the latest.

The build uses the manifest of only the first client that has one (see
[Dependency versions](using-clients.html#dependency-versions)), so keep your
`[compat]` bounds accurate too.
:::

## Tests and CRAN

CRAN's check machines do not have Julia installed, so your package must install
and pass `R CMD check` without a compiled Julia library.

In tests, skip anything that needs the library:

```r
skip_if_not(jlbind::is_bound("mypkg"))
```

In examples, wrap calls that require the library in
`if (jlbind::is_bound("mypkg"))`.

To check your package on GitHub Actions both ways, run:

```r
jlbind::use_jlbind_ci()
```

This writes `.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml`, which runs `R CMD check` on
Linux, Windows and macOS after compiling your package's Julia code with
`build_library()`, and once on Linux without Julia, as CRAN does.

## Types

`@rcall` converts each argument using `from_sexp()` and converts the return
value using `to_sexp()`. The built-in conversions are:

**Single values**

  | Julia                          | R argument                     | R result                         |
  | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------ | -------------------------------- |
  | `String`, `Symbol`             | A single string                | A character vector of length one |
  | `Float64`                      | A single number                | A double                         |
  | `Int64`                        | A single whole number          | A double                         |
  | `Int32`                        | A single whole number          | An integer                       |
  | `Int16`, `Int8`, `UInt16`      | A single whole number in range | An integer                       |
  | `UInt32`                       | A single whole number in range | A double                         |
  | `Float32`, `Float16`           | A single number in range       | A double                         |
  | `Bool`                         | `TRUE` or `FALSE`              | A logical                        |
  | `ComplexF64`                   | A single complex number        | A complex                        |
  | `Date`                         | A single `Date`                | A `Date`                         |
  | `DateTime`                     | A single `POSIXct`             | A `POSIXct` in UTC               |
  | `Union{Missing,T}`             | A value of type `T`, or `NA`   | A value of type `T`, or `NA`     |
  | `Union{Nothing,T}`             | `NULL`, or a value of type `T` | `NULL`, or a value of type `T`   |
  | `Nothing`                      |                                | `NULL`                           |

**Vectors and arrays**

  | Julia                              | R argument                              | R result                      |
  | ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
  | `Vector{String}`, `Vector{Symbol}` | A character vector or factor            | A character vector            |
  | `Vector{Float64}`, `Vector{Int64}` | A numeric vector                        | A double vector               |
  | `Vector{Int32}`                    | A numeric vector of whole numbers       | An integer vector             |
  | Vectors of the smaller types above | A numeric vector in range               | An integer or double vector   |
  | `Vector{Bool}`                     | A logical vector                        | A logical vector              |
  | `Vector{ComplexF64}`               | A complex or numeric vector             | A complex vector              |
  | `Vector{UInt8}`                    | A raw vector                            | A raw vector                  |
  | `Vector{Date}`                     | A `Date` vector                         | A `Date` vector               |
  | `Vector{DateTime}`                 | A `POSIXct` vector                      | A `POSIXct` vector in UTC     |
  | `Vector{Union{Missing,T}}`         | A vector of type `T`, which can have NA | A vector of type `T` with NA  |
  | `RVector{T}`                       | A double, integer or raw vector         | The same vector               |
  | `Matrix{T}`, `Array{T,N}`          | A matrix or array of type `T`           | A matrix or array of type `T` |

**Lists, data frames and references**

  | Julia                              | R argument                         | R result                      |
  | ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
  | Other `Vector`s, `Tuple`s          | A list                             | A list                        |
  | `NamedTuple`                       | A named list, such as a data frame | A named list                  |
  | `RDataFrame`                       | A data frame                       | A data frame                  |
  | `Dict{String,T}`, `Dict{Symbol,T}` | A named list                       | A named list, sorted by name  |
  | `RRef{T}`                          | A reference to a Julia object      | A reference to a Julia object |
  | `Vector{RRef{T}}`                  | A list of references               | A list of references          |

`NA` is an error unless the type is `Union{Missing,T}` or
`Vector{Union{Missing,T}}`, which turn `NA` into `missing` and back. A number
must fit its type, so an `Int16` argument rejects `40000`, and `NaN` is accepted
only where `missing` is. `Int64` results become doubles, since R's integers have
32 bits; return `Int32` for an R integer.

To use `Date` or `DateTime`, add the `Dates` standard library to the binding
package's dependencies.

A `NamedTuple` argument must have exactly the names of its fields, in any order,
so you can pass a data frame as a named tuple of its columns. To take or return
an actual data frame, wrap the columns in an `RDataFrame`. Its type lists the
column names and the type of each column, so a type alias keeps signatures
short:

```julia
const Sales = RDataFrame{(:group, :amount),Tuple{Vector{String},Vector{Float64}}}
const Summary = RDataFrame{(:group, :mean),Tuple{Vector{String},Vector{Float64}}}

function summarise(df::Sales)
    gs = sort(unique(df.group))
    means = [sum(df.amount[df.group .== g]) / count(==(g), df.group) for g in gs]
    return RDataFrame((group = gs, mean = means))
end

@rcall summarise(df::Sales)::Summary
```

```r
summarise(data.frame(group = c("a", "b", "a"), amount = c(1, 2, 3)))
#>   group mean
#> 1     a    2
#> 2     b    2
```

An `RDataFrame` argument must be a data frame (a tibble works too) with exactly
the declared columns, in any order, so select the columns in the R wrapper if
the data frame has others: `summarise(df[c("group", "amount")])`. Its columns
are its properties (`df.group`), and `NamedTuple(df)` returns them as a named
tuple. Each column converts by the usual rules, so a factor column arrives as
strings, and a `Vector{Union{Missing,Float64}}` column allows `NA`. Returning
columns of different lengths is an error.

Errors inside a list name the element, as in `element 2: expected a number`.

Every other conversion copies, so a function given a large vector it only reads
can take an `RVector{Float64}` (or `RVector{Int32}`, `RVector{UInt8}`). That is
an `AbstractVector` viewing R's memory, without checking for `NA`. It is valid
only until the call returns, so don't store it.

A binding package can support additional types by defining methods for
`JLBind.from_sexp(::Type{T}, x::SEXP)` and `JLBind.to_sexp(x::T)`. `JLBind` also
provides helpers for building R objects directly, such as `JLBind.data_frame()`
for a data frame whose columns are not known when the library is compiled. See
the [`JLBind`
source](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/jlbind/tree/main/inst/julia/JLBind/src)
for the existing conversions and helpers.

### Julia objects in R

Sometimes an object is easier to keep in Julia than to convert into an R data
structure. You can pass such objects by reference using `RRef{T}`. R receives an
external pointer to the Julia object, allowing it to be reused across calls. The
object is released when R garbage-collects the reference.

For example, define a mutable Julia object and expose functions that operate on
it (the
[`counterjl`](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/jlbind/tree/main/tests/clients/counterjl)
test client is a complete version of this):

```julia
mutable struct Counter
    n::Int64
end

JLBind.r_class(::Type{Counter}) = "counter"

new_counter(start::Int64) = Counter(start)
increment(c::Counter, by::Int64) = (c.n += by; c.n)

@rcall new_counter(start::Int64)::RRef{Counter}
@rcall increment(c::RRef{Counter}, by::Int64)::Int64
```

From R, you can create a counter and update it across calls:

```r
counter <- new_counter(0)
class(counter)
#> [1] "counter"

increment(counter, 2)
#> [1] 2
```

`r_class()` sets the R class of the external pointer, so your package can define
methods such as `print()` for it. An argument declared as `RRef{Counter}` also
checks that the reference points to a `Counter`, rather than accepting an
arbitrary Julia object.

## Errors

If a function called through `@rcall` throws a Julia exception, jlbind turns it
into an R error. The messages from `ArgumentError`, `ErrorException`,
`DimensionMismatch`, `OverflowError`, and `AssertionError` are passed through.
Other exceptions are summarized.

## Compilation constraints (trimming)

By default, jlbind compiles the shared library with `juliac --trim=safe`. This
keeps the compiled image small by including only code reachable from the
functions exposed through `@rcall`. It also requires calls to be resolvable at
compile time.

If your package cannot be compiled with trimming, add the following field to
`DESCRIPTION`:

```text
Config/jlbind/trim: false
```

::: {.callout-warning}
An untrimmed library includes the full Julia system image and is *much* larger,
so avoid it if you can.
:::

### Abstract types

With trimming, a common source of compilation errors is a function that accepts
several concrete types through an abstract `RRef`. Suppose your binding package
works with shapes:

<details>
<summary>Shape types and their areas</summary>

```julia
abstract type Shape end

struct Circle <: Shape
    radius::Float64
end
struct Square <: Shape
    side::Float64
end
struct Rectangle <: Shape
    width::Float64
    height::Float64
end
struct Triangle <: Shape
    base::Float64
    height::Float64
end

JLBind.r_class(::Type{<:Shape}) = "shape"

area(s::Circle) = pi * s.radius^2
area(s::Square) = s.side^2
area(s::Rectangle) = s.width * s.height
area(s::Triangle) = s.base * s.height / 2
```

</details>

An entrypoint that takes an `RRef{Shape}` knows only that its argument is *some*
`Shape`. If it simply calls `area(s)`, the compiler cannot tell which of the
four methods that call reaches, and the build fails with an error such as:

```text
Verifier error #1: unresolved call from statement area(s::Shape)::Any
```

One possible solution is to branch on the concrete types once, with
`@nospecialize`, and to make the call inside each branch, where the type is
known:

```julia
function with_shape(f::F, @nospecialize(s::Shape)) where {F}
    s isa Circle && return f(s)
    s isa Square && return f(s)
    s isa Rectangle && return f(s)
    s isa Triangle && return f(s)
    throw(ArgumentError("unknown shape"))
end

circle(radius::Float64) = Circle(radius)
square(side::Float64) = Square(side)
rectangle(width::Float64, height::Float64) = Rectangle(width, height)
triangle(base::Float64, height::Float64) = Triangle(base, height)
shape_area(@nospecialize(s::Shape)) = with_shape(area, s)
scaled_area(@nospecialize(s::Shape), factor::Float64) =
    with_shape(x -> factor^2 * area(x), s)

@rcall circle(radius::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall square(side::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall rectangle(width::Float64, height::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall triangle(base::Float64, height::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall shape_area(shape::RRef{Shape})::Float64
@rcall scaled_area(shape::RRef{Shape}, factor::Float64)::Float64
```

Every shape can then be passed to the same generated R functions:

```r
shapes <- list(circle(1), square(2), rectangle(2, 3), triangle(2, 3))
vapply(shapes, shape_area, numeric(1))
#> [1] 3.141593 4.000000 6.000000 3.000000

scaled_area(square(2), 3)
#> [1] 36
```

Without `@nospecialize`, Julia compiles a separate `with_shape` for each
concrete shape, and the call into it can't be resolved, for the same reason as
`area(s)`. Functions that pass the shape on, such as `shape_area`, need it too
(this small example happens to compile without it, since it is inlined).

If a hierarchy has only a few types, some alternatives to `@nospecialize` are:

- Declare a separate entrypoint for each concrete type
  (`RRef{Circle}`,`RRef{Square}`, ...) and choose between them in R.

- Use a small `Union` such as `RRef{Union{Circle,Square}}`, which Julia resolves
  by checking each member in turn.
